claim: Type II CRISPR immune systems in bacteria use a dual RNA-guided DNA endonuclease, Cas9, to cleave foreign DNA at specific sites.
source_text: Type II CRISPR immune systems in bacteria use a dual RNA-guided DNA endonuclease, Cas9, to cleave foreign DNA at specific sites.
evidence_reasoning: This statement reflects established scientific knowledge about bacterial CRISPR systems and is presented as background information, likely supported by prior literature.

claim: Cas9 assembles with hybrid guide RNAs in human cells.
source_text: We show here that Cas9 assembles with hybrid guide RNAs in human cells
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Cas9 can induce the formation of double-strand DNA breaks (DSBs) at a site complementary to the guide RNA sequence in genomic DNA.
source_text: Cas9 assembles with hybrid guide RNAs in human cells and can induce the formation of double-strand DNA breaks (DSBs) at a site complementary to the guide RNA sequence in genomic DNA.
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary experimental finding demonstrated through the Surveyor nuclease assay and other experiments described in the Results section.

claim: Cas9-mediated DNA cleavage activity requires both Cas9 and the complementary binding of the guide RNA.
source_text: This cleavage activity requires both Cas9 and the complementary binding of the guide RNA.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data showing that cleavage does not occur with Cas9 alone or sgRNA alone, as demonstrated in Figure 1E.

claim: RNA expression and/or assembly into Cas9 is the limiting factor for Cas9-mediated DNA cleavage in transfected cells.
source_text: Experiments using extracts from transfected cells show that RNA expression and/or assembly into Cas9 is the limiting factor for Cas9-mediated DNA cleavage.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is based on experimental data from cell lysate experiments (Figure 2) showing that adding in vitro transcribed sgRNA to lysates containing Cas9 restored cleavage activity.

claim: Extension of the RNA sequence at the 3′ end enhances DNA targeting activity in vivo.
source_text: In addition, we find that extension of the RNA sequence at the 3′ end enhances DNA targeting activity in vivo.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data comparing different sgRNA versions (v1.0, v2.1, v2.2) shown in Figure 3.

claim: RNA-programmed genome editing is a facile strategy for introducing site-specific genetic changes in human cells.
source_text: These results show that RNA-programmed genome editing is a facile strategy for introducing site-specific genetic changes in human cells.
evidence_reasoning: This is a conclusion drawn from the collective experimental data demonstrating successful genome editing in human cells using the Cas9-sgRNA system.

claim: Zinc-finger nucleases (ZFNs) and transcription activator-like effector nucleases (TALENs) have proved effective for genomic manipulation.
source_text: Zinc-finger nucleases (ZFNs) and transcription activator-like effector nucleases (TALENs) have proved effective for such genomic manipulation
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge from prior research, supported by citations (Urnov et al., 2010; Bogdanove and Voytas, 2011).

claim: The use of ZFNs and TALENs has been limited by the need to engineer a specific protein for each dsDNA target site and by off-target activity.
source_text: but their use has been limited by the need to engineer a specific protein for each dsDNA target site and by off-target activity

claim: CRISPR/Cas loci encode RNA-guided adaptive immune systems that can destroy foreign DNA.
source_text: Research into genome defense mechanisms in bacteria showed that CRISPR (Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats)/Cas (CRISPR-associated) loci encode RNA-guided adaptive immune systems that can destroy foreign DNA
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge from prior research, supported by multiple citations (Bhaya et al., 2011; Terns and Terns, 2011; Wiedenheft et al., 2012).

claim: Type II CRISPR/Cas systems require a single protein, Cas9, to catalyze DNA cleavage.
source_text: The Type II CRISPR/Cas systems require a single protein, Cas9, to catalyze DNA cleavage
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge from prior research, supported by citation (Sapranauskas et al., 2011).

claim: Cas9 generates blunt DSBs at sites defined by a 20-nucleotide guide sequence contained within an associated CRISPR RNA (crRNA) transcript.
source_text: Cas9 generates blunt DSBs at sites defined by a 20-nucleotide guide sequence contained within an associated CRISPR RNA (crRNA) transcript
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge from prior research, supported by citations (Gasiunas et al., 2012; Jinek et al., 2012).

claim: Cas9 requires both the guide crRNA and a trans-activating crRNA (tracrRNA) that is partially complementary to the crRNA for site-specific DNA recognition and cleavage.

evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge from prior research, supported by citations (Deltcheva et al., 2011; Jinek et al., 2012).

claim: The crRNA:tracrRNA complex can be redesigned as a single transcript (single-guide RNA or sgRNA) encompassing the features required for both Cas9 binding and DNA target site recognition.

evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge from prior research, supported by citation (Jinek et al., 2012).

claim: Using sgRNA, Cas9 can be programmed to cleave double-stranded DNA at any site defined by the guide RNA sequence and including a GG protospacer-adjacent (PAM) motif.

claim: It was not known whether the bacterial Cas9 system would function in eukaryotic cells.
source_text: However, it was not known whether such a bacterial system would function in eukaryotic cells.
evidence_reasoning: This statement reflects the state of knowledge prior to this study, identifying a gap in the literature.

claim: Cas9 can be expressed and localized to the nucleus of human cells.
source_text: We show here that Cas9 can be expressed and localized to the nucleus of human cells
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by Western blot analysis (Figure 1A) and fluorescence microscopy (Figure 1B) showing nuclear localization of Cas9-HA-NLS-GFP.

claim: Cas9 assembles with sgRNA in vivo.
source_text: and that it assembles with sgRNA in vivo
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the functional activity of Cas9 in cells co-transfected with sgRNA, as demonstrated by the Surveyor assay and cleavage experiments.

claim: Cas9:sgRNA complexes can generate double stranded breaks and stimulate non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) repair in genomic DNA at a site complementary to the sgRNA sequence.
source_text: These complexes can generate double stranded breaks and stimulate non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) repair in genomic DNA at a site complementary to the sgRNA sequence
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by the Surveyor nuclease assay (Figure 1E) and Sanger sequencing of clonal amplicons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) showing indels characteristic of NHEJ repair.

claim: Cas9-mediated genomic DNA cleavage activity requires both Cas9 and the sgRNA.
source_text: an activity that requires both Cas9 and the sgRNA
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by control experiments showing no cleavage with Cas9 alone or sgRNA alone (Figure 1E).

claim: sgRNA assembly into Cas9 is the limiting factor for Cas9-mediated DNA cleavage in transfected cells.

evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experiments showing that lysates from Cas9-transfected cells could cleave target DNA when supplemented with in vitro transcribed sgRNA (Figure 2).

evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated by the Surveyor nuclease assay showing cleavage products at the expected position (Figure 1E).

claim: The Surveyor nuclease assay can detect minor insertions and deletions in a genomic locus resulting from imperfect repair by DSB-induced NHEJ.
source_text: To do this, we probed for minor insertions and deletions in the locus resulting from imperfect repair by DSB-induced NHEJ using the Surveyor nuclease assay
evidence_reasoning: This describes an established method, supported by citation (Qiu et al., 2004).

claim: DNA repair by NHEJ is typically induced by a DSB.
source_text: As DNA repair by NHEJ is typically induced by a DSB, a positive signal in the Surveyor assay indicates that genomic DNA cleavage has occurred.

claim: Two new versions of the CLTA1 sgRNA were designed to include an additional 4 or 10 base pairs in the helix that mimics the base-pairing interactions between the crRNA and tracrRNA.
